steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on quickly evaluating the worst robustness of complex networks. Explain connectivity robustness and why worst-case robustness matters, why existing attacks and percolation models fall short, and introduce our MDA-based framework with the adapted CNN-SPP, its extensions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Connectivity robustness and how it is assessed (GCC size sequence)
2. Worst robustness: why it matters and why existing attacks/models cannot capture it
3. Most Destruction Attack (MDA) as a suboptimal solution
4. Speeding it up with adapted CNN-SPP; the WRE framework
5. Extensibility and paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Robustness
- connectivity robustness: networked system keeps structural integrity under random failures or malicious attacks
- structural integrity = necessary condition for normal operation
- assessment fundamental for topology design, vulnerability analysis, functional maintenance
- percolation theory: value sequence of residual network characteristic during failure/attack
- four types of assessment methods; most prevalent: change in size of giant connected component (GCC); simple, direct, scale of functioning core

2. Worst robustness
- crucial real-world question: network's worst-case robustness; limit under most destructive attacks; lower bound = "Worst Robustness"
- needed for defense against unknown attacks, costs of security design and maintenance
- existing research relies on attack paradigms; destructive but not necessarily worst
- attack types: node centrality, percolation, cascading failures, iterative adaptive methods, heuristic strategies, machine learning methods
- percolation models on random graphs: exact expressions for GCC appearance etc., non-Poissonian or completely general degree distributions; only near phase transition; no whole-process view, no worst robustness

3. MDA
- network dismantling, optimal attacks also pursue limit; no singular/analytical solution except enumeration
- reframe: dismantle network for fastest GCC decrease; NP-hard, impractical for large networks -> suboptimal solutions urgent
- existing strategies may be most damaging at certain stages/sections
- knowledge stacking: take most destructive parts of each known strategy -> complete continuous strategy with maximum known destructive power
- Most Destruction Attack (MDA), Figure 1; no single/combined attack exceeds it -> robustness under MDA = worst robustness
- any system, any component failure (nodes, edges); universally applicable suboptimal solution

4. CNN-SPP + WRE
- MDA time-consuming -> adapted CNN-SPP (well-validated deep learning algorithm); trained on MDA results -> rapid, accurate assessment
- scope: connectivity robustness, node failures; rationality validation of MDA; efficiency via adapted CNN-SPP
- results on networks with diverse topological features: effective, efficient
- Worst Robustness Evaluation Framework (WRE framework): guides security design and protection cost budgets until theoretical optimum found; infrastructure and adversarial networks

5. Extensions + outline
- approximating optimal solution, enhancing predictive capabilities; broad generality
- edge failures; optimal control robustness: replace attack strategies / GCC sequences with control strategies and network synchronization metrics
- crucial node identification
- Sec. 2 framework, Sec. 3 results and analysis, Sec. 4 discussion and extensions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Robustness, and specifically connectivity robustness, is the ability of a networked system to keep its structural integrity when it faces random component failures or malicious external attacks. Here, keeping a certain level of structural integrity is seen as a necessary condition for the network to keep operating normally. For almost any such system, assessing its robustness accurately is a basic concern in the design of its topological architecture, in vulnerability analysis, and in functional maintenance. Based on percolation theory, a sequence of values that represents a specific characteristic of the residual network is commonly used to assess the robustness of a network during failure or attack. These assessment methods can be put into four types, and the most common one is the sequence of changes in the size of the giant connected component (GCC) of the network. This sequence is simple and direct, and it reflects the scale of the core network that keeps functioning during failure or attack.

In practice, a more important and pressing real-world question is how a network does in its worst-case scenario in terms of robustness. That is, the limit of robustness a system shows when it is hit by the most destructive attacks. We call the lower bound of this robustness “Worst Robustness”. Only by understanding the worst robustness of a system can we assess more accurately how well it can defend against unknown attacks and work out the costs of designing and maintaining its security. But existing research on robustness often depends on one or more potential attack paradigms. Even if these attacks are quite destructive, they may not represent the worst robustness of the system. This is true no matter whether the attack strategies are based on node centrality, percolation, cascading failures, iterative adaptive methods, heuristic strategies, or machine learning methods. On the other hand, percolation models on random graphs can give exact expressions for the position where the GCC appears and other topological statistics, whether the degree distribution of the network is non-Poissonian or completely general, but they often only look at the area near the phase transition. Such models cannot evaluate the overall performance of network robustness over the whole process, and they cannot answer the question of worst robustness.

Studies on network dismantling and optimal attacks are also basically looking for this limit state, but what we know so far does not give a singular or analytical solution to the problem, other than enumerating all the possibilities. The worst robustness problem can be reframed as the question of how to dismantle a network most effectively so that its GCC size drops the fastest. Looking for its exact solution directly is impractical since it is an NP-hard problem, especially for large-scale networks. So finding better ways to capture suboptimal solutions is an urgent issue with practical significance. Existing dismantling strategies may not give optimal solutions, but they might be able to cause the most severe damage at a certain stage or in specific sections. Motivated by this, and based on the concept of knowledge stacking, we can take the most destructive parts of each known strategy and put them together into a complete, continuous strategy that has the maximum known destructive power over the whole process. We define this strategy as the Most Destruction Attack (MDA), as shown in Figure 1. By this definition, no single or combined attack strategy can cause more damage than MDA. So the robustness the network shows under MDA can be defined as the worst robustness. For any networked system and any type of component failure (such as nodes or edges), the worst robustness can be captured by simulating MDA. This makes the approach a universally applicable and available suboptimal solution.

4. Speeding up with adapted CNN-SPP
- MDA evaluation time-consuming; adapted, well-validated deep learning algorithm (adapted CNN-SPP)
- trained on MDA results -> rapid, accurate worst robustness assessment

5. Summary of the paper
- connectivity robustness, node failures; MDA concept; rationality validation; adapted CNN-SPP for efficiency
- diverse topologies: effective and efficient
- WRE framework: guides security design and protection cost budgets until theoretical optimum; infrastructure + adversarial networks

6. Extensibility
- approximating optimal solution, predictive capabilities; broad generality
- edge failures; optimal control robustness (control strategies, synchronization capability metrics)
- crucial node identification

7. Outline: Sec. 2 framework, Sec. 3 results, Sec. 4 discussion

For any networked system and any type of component failure (such as nodes or edges), the worst robustness can be captured by simulating MDA. This makes the approach a universally applicable and available suboptimal solution.

Evaluating the worst robustness of networks with MDA takes a lot of time, so to deal with this we introduce an adapted and well-validated deep learning algorithm, called adapted CNN-SPP. By training the adapted CNN-SPP thoroughly on the results from MDA, we get a fast and accurate assessment of the worst robustness of the network.

In the setting of connectivity robustness under node failures, this paper deals with the problem of the worst robustness of a network and introduces the concept of MDA so that a practical and feasible assessment of the worst robustness is possible. We validate that MDA is rational and then make the assessment more efficient by using an adapted CNN-SPP model. The results on networks with different topological features show that the framework is effective and efficient. Until the theoretical optimum solution is found, the Worst Robustness Evaluation Framework (WRE framework) will be essential for guiding system security design and protection cost budgets. This is true both for infrastructure networks and for adversarial networks, and it has significant practical implications.

Finally, the paper discusses how the WRE framework can be extended in terms of approximating the optimal solution and enhancing predictive capabilities. The performance boundary issues that the WRE framework deals with are very general. Besides scenarios with edge failures, the WRE framework can be applied to the rapid assessment of the optimal control robustness of a network. In that case one only needs to replace the attack strategies and the GCC size change sequences with control strategies and the matching network synchronization capability evaluation metrics. This paradigm also has significant potential for crucial node identification.

The rest of the article is organized as follows. Sec. 2 presents the proposed worst robustness evaluation framework, and Sec. 3 shows our results and analysis. Finally, Sec. 4 discusses the study and its extensions in terms of performance and applications.

steps.text:

In this context, maintaining a certain level of structural integrity is considered a necessary condition for the network to sustain its normal operation. For nearly any such system, accurately assessing its robustness is a fundamental concern in the design of its topological architecture [4,5,6], vulnerability analysis [7,8], and functional maintenance [9]. Grounded in percolation theory [10], a value sequence representing a specific characteristic of the residual network is commonly employed to assess the robustness of a network during failure or attack. These assessment methods can be categorized into four types [11], the most prevalent being the sequence of changes in the size of the giant connected component (GCC) of the network. This simple and direct sequence reflects the scale of the core network that continues to function amidst failure or attack.

In practice, a more crucial and pressing real-world question is how a network performs in its worst-case scenario in terms of robustness, that is, the limit of robustness exhibited by a system when subjected to the most destructive attacks. We term the lower bound of this robustness “Worst Robustness”. Only by comprehending the worst robustness of a system can we more accurately assess its defensive capabilities against unknown attacks and determine the costs associated with the design and maintenance of its security [12]. However, existing research on robustness often relies on one or more potential attack paradigms. Even if these attacks exhibit considerable destructiveness, they may not represent the system’s worst robustness. This holds regardless of whether the attack strategies are based on node centrality [1,13,14,15,16,17], percolation [18,19,20], cascading failures [21,22], iterative adaptive methods [23,24], heuristic strategies [25,26,27], or machine learning methods [28,29,30]. Such models cannot evaluate the overall performance of network robustness throughout the entire process and thus cannot address the question of worst robustness.

While studies on network dismantling [33,34] and optimal attacks [26,35] are also fundamentally pursuing this limit state, existing knowledge fails to provide a singular or analytical solution to this issue, aside from enumerating all possibilities. The problem of worst robustness can be reframed as the question of how to most effectively dismantle a network so as to induce the fastest decrease in its GCC size. Directly seeking its exact solution is impractical, as it is an NP-hard problem, particularly for large-scale networks. Therefore, finding better ways to capture its suboptimal solutions becomes an urgent and practically significant issue. Motivated by this insight and based on the concept of knowledge stacking, we extract the most destructive parts of each known strategy and assemble them into a complete, continuous strategy with the maximum known destructive power throughout the entire process. We define this strategy as the Most Destruction Attack (MDA), as shown in Figure 1. By this definition, the damage caused by any single or combined attack strategy cannot exceed that of MDA, and therefore the robustness exhibited by the network under MDA can be defined as its worst robustness. Given any networked system and any type of component failure (such as nodes or edges), the worst robustness can be captured through MDA simulation. This approach thus offers a universally applicable and available suboptimal solution.

To further address the time-consuming nature of evaluating the worst robustness of networks using MDA, we introduce an adapted and well-validated deep learning algorithm, known as adapted CNN-SPP [11]. By comprehensively training the adapted CNN-SPP with the results derived from MDA, we achieve a rapid and accurate assessment of the network’s worst robustness.

In the context of connectivity robustness under node failure scenarios, this paper addresses the problem of the network’s worst robustness and introduces the concept of MDA to enable a practical and feasible assessment of it. We establish the rationality validation of MDA and subsequently enhance the efficiency of the assessment by invoking an adapted CNN-SPP model. Results on networks with diverse topological features demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this framework. Until the theoretical optimum solution is identified, the Worst Robustness Evaluation Framework (WRE framework) will be imperative in guiding system security design and protection cost budgets, for both infrastructure networks and adversarial networks, which carries significant practical implications.

Finally, the paper discusses the extensibility of the WRE framework in terms of approximating the optimal solution and enhancing predictive capabilities. The performance boundary issues addressed by the WRE framework have broad generality. In addition to scenarios involving edge failures, the WRE framework applies to the rapid assessment of a network’s optimal control robustness; here, one only needs to replace the attack strategies and GCC size change sequences with control strategies [14,36,37] and the corresponding network synchronization capability evaluation metrics [38,39]. Moreover, this paradigm holds significant potential for crucial node identification [14].

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Sec. 2 presents the proposed worst robustness evaluation framework, and Sec. 3 showcases our results and analysis. Finally, Sec. 4 discusses the study and its extensions in terms of performance and applications.
